document.title: Protest and Comments of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC in response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s 02/23/2026 60-Day Compliance Filing

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.
) 
Docket No. ER26-1479-000 
PROTEST AND COMMENTS OF CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC  
Constellation1 protests limited provisions in PJM’s Sixty-Day Compliance Filing2 that are 
non-compliant with the Commission’s December 18, 2025 Order3 because they fail “to make the 
directed changes.”4 First, the replacement of “Point of Interconnection” in the definition of Co-
Located Load with “Point of Change in Ownership” contradicts the Commission’s order. Second, 
the proposed Behind the Meter Generation (“BTMG”) rules expand BTMG to include a 50-MW 
threshold and thus create a large class of favored resources at the expense of Co-Located Load. 
Constellation also seeks clarification of PJM’s filing in several other areas to ensure compliance, 
to accelerate the interconnection of large loads, and to prevent undue discrimination against Co-
Located Load and the generators seeking to serve it. 
PROTEST 
In two important areas, PJM’s proposal is outside the scope of compliance, falls short of 
the Commission’s intent, and perpetuates existing undue discrimination that has delayed the 
interconnection of large loads for years. 
 
1 Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) files this protest pursuant to Rule 211 of the Commission’s 
Rules of Practice and Procedure. 18 C.F.R. § 385.211 (2025). 
2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Sixty-Day Compliance Filing for Co-Located Load Related Revisions to Open Access 
Transmission Tariff to Comply with Commission Order in Docket No. EL25-49-000, et al., Docket No. ER26-1479-
000 (Feb. 23, 2026) (“Sixty-Day Compliance Filing”). 
3 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025) (“December 18th Order”). 
4 NorthWestern Corp., 113 FERC ¶ 61,215, at P 9 (2005) (“The Commission has long established that compliance 
filings must be limited to the specific directives ordered by the Commission. The purpose of a compliance filing is 
to make the directed changes and the Commission’s focus in reviewing them is whether or not they comply with the 
Commission’s previously-stated directives.”); see also Cal. Power Exch. Corp., 101 FERC ¶ 61,330, at P 25 (2002) 
(“The purpose of a compliance filing is to make only the revisions directed by the Commission.”).

2 
I. 
The Commission Should Reject PJM’s New Definition of Co-Located Load as Outside 
the Scope of Compliance, or in the Alternative, Require Further Modification 
As with PJM’s Thirty-Day Compliance Filing,5 the Commission should reject PJM’s 
proposal to use its Sixty-Day Compliance Filing to replace the Commission-mandated “Point of 
Interconnection” in the definition of Co-Located Load with the “Point of Change in Ownership.”6 
Changing the specific definition of Co-Located Load already approved by the Commission is 
outside the scope of compliance. The December 18th Order adopted the following definition of 
Co-Located Load: “a ‘configuration [that] refers to end-use customer load that is physically 
connected to the facilities of an existing or planned Customer Facility on the Interconnection 
Customer’s side of the Point of Interconnection to the PJM Transmission System.’”7 The 
Commission neither sought comment on nor directed PJM to propose a new definition of Co-
Located Load. Nor did the December 18th Order permit PJM to propose variations that PJM 
considered were “consistent with or superior to” the Commission’s adopted definition as the 
Commission does with amendments to the pro forma Generator Interconnection Agreements.8 
 
5 See Comments and Conditional Protest of Constellation Energy, Docket No. ER26-1088-000 (Feb. 10, 2026) 
(“Constellation’s Thirty-Day Compliance Filing Comments”); id. at 5 (“The Commission must ensure that 
Transmission Owners are not permitted to exploit the interconnection process to continue to deny, delay, encumber, 
or tie interconnection services for large load configurations that they disfavor. Accordingly, the Commission should 
reject PJM’s new definition of Co-Located Load.”). 
6 See Sixty-Day Compliance Filing at 31-35; id. at Exhibit B (“Marked Tariff”) at 12, 74-75, 81-82. 
7 December 18th Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 164. 
8 Non-RTO/ISO transmission providers seeking deviations from the pro forma generator interconnection procedures 
and agreements must demonstrate that such deviations are “consistent with or superior to” the pro forma provisions. 
See Standardization of Generator Interconnection Agreements and Procedures, Order No. 2003, 104 FERC 
¶ 61,103, at PP 825-26 (2003) (establishing the “consistent with or superior to” standard for non-RTO/ISO 
transmission providers seeking variations from the pro forma Large Generator Interconnection Process (“LGIP”) 
and Large Generator Interconnection Agreement (“LGIA”), drawing from the approach taken in Order No. 888 for 
variations from the OATT); Reform of Generator Interconnection Procedures and Agreements, Order No. 845, 163 
FERC ¶ 61,043, at P 43 (2018) (confirming that non-RTO/ISO transmission providers must justify variations as 
“consistent with or superior to” the pro forma LGIP or LGIA); Improvements to Generator Interconnection 
Procedures and Agreements, Order No. 2023, 184 FERC ¶ 61,054, at P 10 (2023) (continuing to apply the 
“consistent with or superior to” standard for non-RTO/ISO transmission providers).

3 
Consistent with the Federal Power Act and longstanding Commission precedent, if PJM “wished 
to depart from or challenge” the Commission’s adoption of PJM’s definition of Co-Located Load, 
it “should have filed for rehearing” of the December 18th Order.9 PJM did not do so. In fact, PJM 
had multiple opportunities to express concerns with the Commission “adopt[ing] PJM’s 
definition.”10 The Commission should “not allow [PJM] to pursue such matters on compliance” 
and should reject PJM’s departure from the Order.11 
Subsequent discussions between PJM and Constellation have not resolved Constellation’s 
concerns regarding PJM’s definition.12 The “Point of Change in Ownership” definition will not 
“afford[] greater certainty to all interconnection parties.”13 PJM overlooks the record evidence of 
discrimination by Transmission Owners against Co-Located Load that does not connect directly 
with the Transmission Owner. Using the “Point of Change in Ownership” could give the 
Transmission Owner an additional tool to discriminate against competing projects.14 Unlike the 
 
9 16 U.S.C. § 825l; see also, e.g., Ne. Utils. Serv. Co., 74 FERC ¶ 61,355, at n.10 (1996).  
10 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115, at PP 3-4 (2025). 
11 Ne. Utils. Serv. Co., 74 FERC ¶ 61,355 at n.10 (“We will direct that these provisos be deleted. They are outside the 
scope of the compliance filing ordered. If the NU companies had wished to depart from or challenge our conditions, 
they should have filed for rehearing. They did not do so and we will not allow them to pursue such matters on 
compliance.”); see also Nev. Power Co., 157 FERC ¶ 61,230, at P 54 (2016) (“We find that Barrick Mines’ 
comments are an attempt to revisit issues the Commission has already decided and are outside the scope of the 
compliance filing. Barrick Mines was a party to the section 206 proceeding and could have sought rehearing of the 
June 9 Order. Instead, their comments in this compliance filing proceeding constitute a collateral attack on the 
June 9 Order.”) (emphasis added). 
12 See Sixty-Day Compliance Filing at 33 (stating that “these concerns have benefited from discussion and further 
consideration”). PJM has not withdrawn its new definition of Co-Located Load. 
13 Id. at 33-34. 
14 See, e.g., Complaint Requesting Fast Track Processing of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, Constellation 
Energy Generation, LLC v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. EL25-20-000 at 7 (Nov. 22, 2024) (“Exelon 
is refusing to process necessary studies on these grounds, demanding expensive upgrades under their unfiled 
interconnection procedures, delaying agreed-upon work which will force a nuclear plant to take additional outages, 
and forcing additional services to be procured.”) (“Constellation Complaint”); id at 7-8. (“Exelon fulfilled its 
responsibilities as an interconnection provider to review PJM’s necessary studies for one Constellation nuclear 
station, the LaSalle Clean Energy Center (‘LaSalle’), but later refused to do so at the other two stations, insisting 
that Constellation or its potential customer must first apply for retail service and designate what sort of wholesale

4 
“Point of Change in Ownership,” the “Point of Interconnection” is a defined physical point where 
the Interconnection Facilities connect to the grid.15 If parties cannot agree on the location of the 
Point of Interconnection, there is a Tariff process for resolving the disagreement that helps prevent 
discrimination and unreasonable outcomes.16 By contrast, the “Point of Change in Ownership” is 
not a defined physical point. A Transmission Owner could determine that equipment to serve the 
load is not “necessary to physically and electrically interconnect the Generating Facility with the 
 
transmission service it will take from Exelon.”); id. at 17 (“But for Constellation’s … Limerick Clean Energy Center 
(‘Limerick’) in Pennsylvania, Exelon has refused to conduct its review of PJM’s completed necessary studies, 
insisting that Constellation or its potential customer must first apply for retail service and designate what sort of 
wholesale transmission service it will take from Exelon.”); Constellation Complaint at 8 (“projects are being held 
hostage by a few monopolies refusing to cooperate with reliability studies related to interconnection modifications”); 
id. at 10 n.25 (“Exelon refuses to review co-location reliability studies as required by the OATT and pro forma ISA”) 
(citing Constellation PDO Protest, Exhibit 1, Declaration of James R. McCoskey at ¶ 13); id. at 16 (“Proposed Fully 
Isolated Co-Located data center projects in PJM are currently being held hostage by one or two monopoly utilities’ 
refusal to cooperate … with reliability studies related to interconnection modifications.”); see also Supporting 
Comments of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate Transmission 
System, Docket No. RM26-4-000, at 3-4 (Nov. 21, 2025) (“Some Transmission Owners have simply refused to 
participate in PJM’s studies to analyze reliability impacts; and some, acting under unfiled interconnection study 
procedures, have changed their entire construct and timetable for processing load studies.”) (“Constellation ANOPR 
Comments”); Answer of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. et al., Docket Nos. 
EL25-49-000, et al., at 3 (Apr. 23, 2025) (“The Indicated Transmission Owners read the existing Tariff to require 
this one-size-fits-all limitation, and they have refused to perform studies for new load seeking a different 
configuration.”); id. at 7 (“What is more, regardless of what the Tariff actually says and does not say, some of the 
Indicated Transmission Owners have refused to cooperate in PJM’s ‘necessary studies’ process unless the load 
agrees to taking NITS, claiming justification under the Tariff. Some of the Indicated Transmission Owners have 
refused to process necessary studies, demanded expensive upgrades under their unfiled interconnection procedures, 
and forced a generator seeking to serve co-located load to procure additional services not required by the Tariff.”) 
(citing Constellation Complaint at 7); Constellation Complaint at 9 (“Exelon’s also is refusing to perform work on 
LaSalle’s interconnection facilities to accommodate co-location, none of which affects the grid. Exelon’s refusal to 
complete previously agreed-upon work as scheduled during an upcoming planned outage will increase costs to 
Constellation by $15.3- $19 million at that site alone, just so Exelon can pursue its litigation positions.”); see also 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115, at P 75 (“there are allegations in the record that Exelon has 
delayed work on Constellation’s requests to co-locate load with its generators at certain facilities due to Exelon’s 
concerns that such requests are not allowed under the Tariff without arranging for wholesale transmission or retail 
distribution service.”). 
15 OATT, Part VIII.A 400 Definitions (“‘Point of Interconnection’ shall mean the point or points where the 
Interconnection Facilities connect with the Transmission System.’”). 
16 Id. at Part IX.B GIA, Appendix 2 Standard Terms and Conditions, § 2.1 (“The location of the Point of 
Interconnection shall be mutually agreed by the Interconnected Entities, provided, however, that if the 
Interconnected Entities are unable to agree on the Point of Interconnection, the Transmission Provider shall 
determine the Point of Interconnection, provided that Transmission Provider shall not select a Point of 
Interconnection that would impose excessive costs on either of the Interconnected Entities and shall take material 
system reliability considerations into account in such selection.”).

5 
Transmission System,”17 and take the position that the equipment is a Transmission Owner 
Interconnection Facility18 instead of a Project Developer Interconnection Facility. The 
Transmission Owner could assert that the equipment and load both fall on the Transmission 
Owner’s side of the Point of Change in Ownership and no longer qualify as Co-Located Load. 
Below is an illustration of a hypothetical example to demonstrate this point. Even if such claims 
might eventually be overturned by the Commission, changing the definition of Co-Located Load 
would allow Transmission Owners to use the determination of the Point of Change in Ownership 
to cause unnecessary delay or other mischief for large load projects seeking speed to service from 
competitive suppliers. 
 
 
17 Id. at Part VIII.A 400 Definitions (“‘Point of Change in Ownership’ shall mean the point, as set forth Schedule B 
of the Generation Interconnection Agreement, where the Project Developer’s Interconnection Facilities connect to 
the Transmission Owner’s Interconnection Facilities.”). 
18 Id. (“‘Transmission Owner Interconnection Facilities’ shall mean all Interconnection Facilities that are not Project 
Developer Interconnection Facilities.”).

6 
Constellation’s example of a new ring bus configuration added to accommodate a large 
load, included in its Thirty-Day Compliance Filing Comments, illustrates the difference, as shown 
above.19 A ring bus allows the load to access supply from the generation facility and the grid. 
Using the “Point of Interconnection” to define Co-Located Load allows any load connected on the 
ring bus to be included as Co-Located Load—even if the Transmission Owner owns some or all 
of the new facilities on the ring bus. By contrast, using “Point of Change in Ownership” to define 
Co-Located Load could allow a Transmission Owner that owns some or all of the new facilities to 
assert the ring bus is not a Project Developer Interconnection Facility, thereby preventing the load 
from qualifying as a Co-Located Load at all. 
PJM’s justification for using the Point of Change in Ownership misses the mark because it 
ignores the fact that new facilities will need to be added to tie in the new large loads and that 
generators do not have sole control over the configuration of these facilities and instead are subject 
to Transmission Owner and PJM interconnection specifications, with any attempt to dispute 
Transmission Owner requirements resulting in an interconnection delay.  
Indicated Transmission Owners argue that Constellation’s concerns are “unsubstantiated” 
and “speculative.”20 This is incorrect. Significant record evidence shows that the Transmission 
Owners have engaged in discriminatory conduct to frustrate Co-Located Load configurations.21 
This includes, as the Indicated Transmission Owners acknowledge,22 letters sent by a PJM 
Transmission Owner stating it will resume work to allow Co-Located Load arrangements only if 
 
19 Constellation’s Thirty-Day Compliance Filing Comments at 5. 
20 Answer of Indicated PJM Transmission Owners, Docket No. ER26-1088-000, at 2 (Feb. 27, 2026) (“Indicated TO 
Feb. 27 Answer”). The Indicated PJM Transmission Owners are a subset of Transmission Owners in PJM, excluding 
Public Service Electric and Gas Company, for example. 
21 See supra at note 14. 
22 Indicated TO Feb. 27 Answer at 3.

7 
the load submits an application for retail service.23 The Commission made preliminary findings 
regarding this record evidence,24 and it granted Constellation’s Complaint (except with regard to 
Constellation’s replacement rate of placing the PJM Guidance Document on file).25 
The Commission must ensure that Transmission Owners cannot exploit the study and 
interconnection process to continue to deny, delay, encumber, or tie interconnection services for 
large load configurations that they disfavor. Alternatively, if the Commission accepts PJM’s 
proposed change from Point of Interconnection to Point of Change in Ownership, it should also 
adopt the same modifications Constellation proposed in its Thirty-Day Compliance Filing 
Comments, grounded in the Commission’s broad authority to fashion a remedy.26 Specifically, the 
Commission should: 
 Direct PJM to revise its Tariff to provide that PJM will determine the Point of 
Change in Ownership if the parties cannot agree, just as PJM currently does if the 
parties cannot agree on the Point of Interconnection.  
 Establish deadlines for Interconnected Entities to mutually agree to the location for 
Point of Change in Ownership and for PJM to determine the location when mutual 
agreement cannot be reached. 
 
23 See Constellation Complaint, Attachment 1, at 2 (Exelon’s November 12, 2024 Letter) (“We continue to believe 
there is no lawful path to interconnect end use load at LaSalle … without that load taking service as a retail customer 
of ComEd and we cannot continue to review proposals for co-location of end use load at LaSalle … on some other 
basis. Furthermore, we will not be able to perform work at [LaSalle], including work during the upcoming refueling 
outage at LaSalle, without an application for retail service and the design addition identified above.”) (emphasis 
added). 
24 The Commission did preliminarily find that the Transmission Owners had discriminated against co-located load, 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115 at P 75, and the Commission also obviously took numerous steps 
to clarify the rules and otherwise ensure that co-located loads could promptly connect to the grid. See December 18th 
Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 passim. 
25Id. PP 248-49. 
26 See Sixty-Day Compliance Filing at 33 (stating “one stakeholder’s conditional protest in Docket No. ER26-1088-
000 offers another alternative for the Commission to consider in reliance on this Commission authority” “to fashion 
a remedy”).

8 
 Ensure that the location selected for the Point of Change in Ownership does not 
eliminate the load from being Co-Located Load altogether unless the Project 
Developer and Co-Located Load desire it. 
 Not tolerate any discrimination or delay and use its enforcement authority or other 
mechanisms to ensure non-discriminatory open access. 
The substance of these modifications is unopposed.27 The Commission should not delay 
implementing them if PJM’s new definition is accepted so that co-location arrangements can move 
forward as the Commission’s Order envisions, consistent with our national interest in winning the 
AI race.28 
II. 
The Commission Should Reject PJM’s 50-MW Materiality Threshold for BTMG, or in 
the Alternative, Address Constellation’s Arguments on Undue Discrimination 
The December 18th Order stated that because the Commission “direct[ed] changes to 
PJM’s existing BTMG rules” the Commission “decline[d]” to address Constellation’s argument 
“that charging all Eligible Customers taking transmission service on behalf of large Co-Located 
Loads for NITS based on a gross demand basis would be unduly discriminatory because it is 
 
27 See id. (discussion of the definitions of Co-Located Load, including as proposed in the Thirty-Day Compliance 
filing filed on January 20, 2026 in Docket No. ER26-1088-000, not including any reference to Constellation’s 
proposed modifications); Answer of the Indicated Transmission Owners, Docket No. ER26-1088-000, at 2-3 (Feb. 
27, 2026) (did not challenge substance of modifications); Answer and Motion for Leave to Answer of the 
Independent Market Monitor for PJM, Docket No. ER26-1088-000, at 2-3 (Feb. 25, 2026) (same). 
28 See Written Testimony of Laura V. Swett Chairman, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, Before the U.S. 
House of Representatives, Committee on Energy and Commerce, Subcommittee on Energy, at 1-2 (Feb. 3, 2026) 
https://www.ferc.gov/news-events/news/testimony-laura-v-swett-chairman-federal-energy-regulatory-commission-
us-house (“We’re in a global energy arms race created by the rise of technology, its tremendous load growth, and 
our push to onshore manufacturing and jobs. I want the United States to lead that race. This is the moment to cement 
America’s energy leadership.”);  Written Testimony of Lindsay S. See Commissioner, Federal Energy Regulatory 
Commission, Before the U.S. House of Representatives, Committee on Energy and Commerce, Subcommittee on 
Energy, at 3 (Feb. 3, 2026), https://cms.ferc.gov/news-events/news/testimony-lindsay-s-see-commissioner-federal-
energy-regulatory-commission (“our national imperative of speed to power and winning the AI race”); Written 
Testimony of David LaCerte Commissioner, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, Before the U.S. House of 
Representatives, Committee on Energy and Commerce, Subcommittee on Energy, at 1 (Feb. 3, 2026), 
https://cms.ferc.gov/news-events/news/testimony-david-lacerte-commissioner-federal-energy-regulatory-
commission-house ) (“[T]he AI race, and even more importantly, who ultimately wins, will also fundamentally 
transform how Americans engage, transact, and compete on the global stage. The AI race is here and America’s 
power grid is a major battlefield.”).

9 
inconsistent with the treatment of BTMG.”29 PJM’s compliance filing, however, expands 
eligibility for future BTMG to a 50-MW threshold and thus substantially adds to the ability to 
unduly discriminate against Co-Located Load. 
PJM’s 50-MW materiality threshold for BTMG is 150 percent larger than the 20-MW 
threshold suggested by the Commission based on the definition of a Small Generator and 
400 percent larger than the 10-MW threshold it suggested based on PJM’s requirement for 
individual generator metering.30 This broadly expands the availability of new special behind-the-
meter generation arrangements that will be constructed, or will have sufficient backup 
generation,31 to fall under the 50-MW threshold to take advantage of netting, reduce their 
transmission costs and otherwise receive preferential treatment over Co-Located Load. Combined 
with PJM’s proposed legacy treatment,32 the exceptions allowing for netting will swallow the rule 
against it. A vast swath of new PJM generators and loads would be allowed to follow the precise 
BTMG rules that the Commission deemed “unjust and unreasonable.”33 
Under PJM’s proposed 50-MW threshold, a significant number of loads with BTMG would 
be able to take advantage of netting and include backup generation as offsetting BTMG. Such 
 
29 December 18th Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 197 (citing Constellation April 23 Reply Comments at 31). 
30 Id. P 221 (“Although we make no finding in this order on a threshold that would be just and reasonable, we note as 
points of reference that PJM requires any generator larger than 10 MW to be individually metered and that the 
Commission’s definition of a small generator is 20 MW.”) (citations omitted). 
31 See Sixty-Day Compliance Filing at 12-13; Marked Tariff at 49-50, 89-90. 
32 See Sixty-Day Compliance Filing at 8-11; Marked Tariff at 49-50, 89-90. In addition to granting legacy treatment 
to existing retail BTMG with contracts effectuating BTMG arrangements before the issuance of the December 18th 
Order, PJM proposes to grant legacy treatment to existing retail BTMG that “otherwise have QF status.” Sixty-Day 
Compliance Filing at 10. As PJM acknowledges, the December 18th Order “does not reference” Qualifying Facilities 
or the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act of 1978. Id. at 9. Constellation acknowledges that the PJM Industrial 
Customer Coalition has sought rehearing on this issue. While Constellation does not take a position with respect to 
the PJM Industrial Customer Coalition’s request, it does note that an exemption for all Qualifying Facilities would 
be very large indeed. 
33 December 18th Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 179.

10 
treatment is not available to Co-Located Load even though there is “no physical, technical, or 
economic reason why a netting construct should apply differently for customers with behind-the-
meter generation or co-located generation.”34 The December 18th Order required that “Eligible 
Customers that elect to take NITS on behalf of Co-Located Loads … must … take NITS on a gross 
demand basis”35 and PJM’s initial brief has no mechanism for Co-Located Load to offset with 
backup generation.36   
Moreover, none of PJM’s justifications for its 50-MW materiality threshold demonstrate 
that the new threshold is a just and reasonable replacement rate. PJM states the “threshold aligns 
with the PJM Board’s definition of large loads additions,”37 which PJM’s Board is proposing to 
include in Tariff and manual provisions being developed as a result of the Critical Issue Fast Path 
for Large Load Additions.38 However, PJM provides no explanation for why that definition is 
relevant to “reduc[ing] the reliability and resource adequacy risks that large or increasing BTMG 
may pose to PJM.”39  
 
34 Answer of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, Docket No. EL25-49-000, et. al, (April 23, 2025) at Exhibit 2, 
Testimony of Zachary Ming at 55:17-19. 
35 December 18th Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 195; id. P 196 (“[W]e find that it would be unjust and unreasonable 
to allow Eligible Customers taking transmission service on behalf of Co-Located Loads to take NITS on a net 
basis.”).  
36 See Initial Brief of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. EL25-49-000, et. al, at 9 (Feb. 23, 2026) (“A Co-
Located Generating Facility will not always be available (e.g., due to planned or unforced outage). To the extent 
that the gross demand of a Co-Located Load is not covered by the Eligible Customer’s Firm Contract Demand 
Transmission Service, the Eligible Customer must cover the remaining gross demand by applying for Non-Firm 
Contract Demand Transmission Service. In that case, the Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, if PJM 
determines it is available for the requested period, will act as a backup to allow the Co-Located Load to meet its full 
demand, while the portion of the Co-Located Generating Facility dedicated to the Co-Located Load is on outage and 
unable to provide energy.”). 
37 Sixty-Day Compliance Filing at 12. 
38 PJM, Board Decisional Letter on Critical Issue Fast Path – Large Load Additions (Jan. 16, 2026), 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/who-we-are/public-disclosures/2026/20260116-pjm-board-
letter-re-results-of-the-cifp-process-large-load-additions.pdf. 
39 December 18th Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 179.

11 
PJM also states that a 50-MW threshold would “avoid unneeded regulatory uncertainty for 
retail customers whose grid impacts on reliability are more limited”40 and “small or de minimis.”41 
Fifty MWs of power could serve a large town or small city.42 PJM provides no support for this 
claim. In addition, PJM argues that “many of the existing Retail BTMG are decades old and may 
need significant upgrades prior to directly interconnecting into the PJM system,” but “given the 
costs associated with such significant upgrades, the owners of such resources may decide to forgo 
the option of interconnecting into the PJM system altogether.”43 PJM again provides no support. 
Nor does PJM explain how exempting load backed by capacity presumably unsuitable for 
interconnection furthers the Commission’s goal of “reduc[ing] the reliability and resource 
adequacy risks that large or increasing BTMG may pose to PJM.”44 
PJM’s 50-MW materiality threshold is unsupported and does not address Constellation’s 
undue discrimination arguments. The Commission should reject the threshold and direct further 
compliance or require alternative modifications to address undue discrimination.  
COMMENTS 
There are several other areas in the PJM compliance filing where clarification is needed or 
appropriate to ensure compliance with the December 18th Order.

41 Id. 
42 See also The Law Dictionary, https://thelawdictionary.org/?s=de+minimis (defining “de minimis” as “a Latin phrase 
that means of a trifling consequence and a matter that is so small that the court does not wish to even consider it.”).

12 
I. 
The Commission Should Require PJM to Clarify the Necessary Studies Process for 
Project Developers to Ensure Speed to Market 
To achieve speed to market, we recommend three clarifications to PJM’s proposed 
Necessary Studies Tariff language: (1) clarify the scope of the Necessary Studies analysis to ensure 
Project Developers are able provide the required information for PJM to timely complete its 
reviews; (2) clarify Project Developers with existing Necessary Studies for Co-Located Load 
arrangements do not have to restart the Necessary Studies process and be further delayed; and 
(3) establish deadlines to complete the Necessary Studies process expeditiously and accelerate the 
interconnection of Co-Located Loads.45  
A. Additional Clarification on the Scope of the Necessary Studies Process Is 
Needed 
Additional clarity is needed regarding the scope of the Necessary Studies to be performed 
by PJM to ensure that Project Developers are able to provide the models and other information 
required for PJM to timely complete the Necessary Studies process.46 PJM proposes to define the 
scope of the Necessary Studies to “include thermal, short circuit, and stability studies under various 
seasonal and load conditions, as specified in more detail in the PJM Manuals.”47 It is not clear 
whether PJM is proposing to use the existing Necessary Studies process or a new process. In 
addition, the Necessary Study Agreement requirements set forth in PJM Manual 14C do not 
specifically reference the studies to be performed. To achieve the Commission’s goal of 
 
45 As PJM filed shells of the Service Agreements for the Interim Network Integration Transmission Service and 
Contract Demand Service, we reserve our ability to comment on any necessary studies requirements. 
46 See PJM Manual 14C, § 1.9. 
47 See OATT, Part IV, Subpart G, § 2 (“Subject to this NSA, sections 4 through 14, Project Developer shall provide 
sufficient information regarding the Planned Modifications, including but not limited to relevant data, drawings, 
models, plans, and specifications, to enable Transmission Provider to evaluate the impact, if any, on the 
Transmission System of the Planned Modifications.”

13 
“provid[ing] additional clarity and transparency”48 and ensuring timely interconnection, the 
Commission should direct PJM to explain in a compliance filing the specific provisions in the PJM 
Manuals to which it refers when PJM’s proposed language states, “as specified in more detail in 
the PJM Manuals.” 
In addition, the proposed Tariff’s scope of the analysis should also be revised to explicitly 
relate to transmission system reliability, consistent with the Commission’s direction. The 
Commission “direct[ed] PJM to revise its Tariff to clarify the procedures for the study necessary 
to determine any modifications to interconnection facilities or Network Upgrades to the 
transmission system PJM finds are needed to maintain transmission system reliability as a result 
of the Interconnection Customer’s request to modify its interconnection service level for an 
existing generating facility to serve Co-Located Load.”49 The Commission was deliberate in 
wording this requirement to relate to transmission system reliability only, compared to other 
requirements in the December 18th Order where the Commission considered both transmission 
reliability and resource adequacy.50  
To further this intent, Constellation proposes the below additions to the language at Tariff 
Part VIII, Subpart A, Section 401 (H)(3)(b)(ii) and (iii): 
ii. Necessary Studies to be performed by Transmission Provider 
include thermal, short circuit, and stability studies under various 
seasonal and load conditions, as specified in more detail in the PJM 
Manuals. Transmission Provider shall assess the impact on 
maintaining transmission system reliability of the reduction in

This clarification must be made in the Tariff. The scope of the Necessary Studies analysis, which 
will determine the upgrades required, “significantly affect[s] rates, terms and conditions” of 
service and is “readily susceptible to specification.”51 It should not be placed in PJM’s business 
manuals where PJM has unilateral discretion.  
B. New Requirements Regarding Necessary Studies Should Not Retroactively 
Apply to Existing Necessary Studies 
The PJM proposed Tariff language includes a new requirement that “Project Developer 
provide Transmission Provider with all information needed to perform the Necessary Studies” 
including “the type of Transmission Service the Eligible Customer will take on behalf of the Co-
Located Load.”52 As this was not a requirement previously, existing study requests will not include 
this information. Constellation requests clarification that Project Developers who have already 
 
51 Energy Storage Ass’n v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 162 FERC ¶ 61,296 (2018). 
52 Marked Tariff, Part VII, Subpart A, section 401.H.3.b.(i)(b).

15 
submitted requests for Necessary Studies prior to implementation of these new requirements will 
be allowed to rely on the results of those studies to the extent relevant in light of the transmission 
service their co-located load plans to request. For example, to the extent that a generator submitted 
a Necessary Study for a co-located load and notified PJM of its intent to delist its capacity (as 
those were the rules in place at the time), and the study showed that no network upgrades beyond 
a capacitor bank were needed, the Project Developer and Co-Located Load should not be forced 
to return to square one and wait for new Necessary Studies to be completed. 
Generators such as Constellation that attempted in good faith to follow the process and 
were stymied by a transmission owner’s refusal to cooperate should not be forced to wait for new 
Necessary Studies to be completed. It is a foundational principle of American administrative law 
that “retroactivity is not favored in the law,” and that “administrative rules will not be construed 
to have retroactive effect unless their language requires this result.”53 This avoidance of retroactive 
impact principle is solidly embodied in sections 205 and 206 of the Federal Power Act through the 
filed-rate doctrine and rule against retroactive ratemaking. The retroactive application of new 
regulatory requirements would effectively penalize parties for failing to comply with rules that did 
not exist at the time they acted—an outcome fundamentally at odds with the rule of law. Preserving 
the progress made for projects already in process on the Necessary Studies is imperative given the 
extensive timelines associated with completing the study (approximately one year), modifying the 
generator interconnection agreement, and constructing any interconnection facilities. Currently it 
takes PJM seven to ten years to complete the study process and build all the transmission upgrades

necessary to provide NITS to a hyperscale data center.54 Co-location, and particularly the Firm 
Contract Demand Service that requires delisting, were designed to provide a more expeditious 
approach, consistent with reliability. Resetting the existing and on-going processes for Necessary 
Studies to retroactively apply the new Tariff requirements to Project that have already submitted 
their study requests is inconsistent with reason, law, and national policy. The Commission should 
clarify that existing studies processes will not be required to pay and wait for a second study to 
meet the new requirements. 
C. Speed to Market Demands Deadlines for Completing the Necessary Studies 
Process 
The Commission ruled that its designation of “Eligible Customer” would render requests 
that the Commission “require transmission owners to cooperate in the necessary stud[ies] process 
… unnecessary.”55 PJM’s compliance language does not resolve these concerns that transmission 
owners could use their natural monopoly market power to delay other parties’ projects. 
Specifically, PJM’s proposed requirement that “[t]he Eligible Customer has been designated to 
take transmission service on behalf of a Co-Located Load in the Application and Study Agreement 
or the Generation Interconnection Agreement”56 does nothing to reduce concerns about, or affect, 
how transmission owners approach Interconnection Customer’s requests to use their generating 
facilities. Nor have existing Tariff provisions requiring the Interconnection Customer or the 
Transmission Owner to not withhold, condition, or delay agreement on modifications to facilities

been a successful deterrent.57 The delays associated with the Transmission Owners’ refusal to 
process Necessary Studies are well documented in the record.58 These delays could continue unless 
Transmission Owners are clearly required to do otherwise. To achieve speed to market, there must 
be deadlines set forth in the Tariff to prevent needless and discriminatory delays. 
II. 
The Proposed Definition of Co-Located Generating Facility Should Be Limited to the 
Portion of a Facility Serving Co-Located Load, Consistent with the Commission’s 
Direction 
The Commission should direct that PJM modify its proposed definition of “Co-Located 
Generating Facility” to confirm compliance with the December 18th Order. PJM proposes to 
define “Co-Located Generating Facility” as “an existing or planned Generating Facility that is 
physically connected to a Co-Located Load.”59 PJM’s proposed definition could be interpreted as 
applying to the entire Generating Facility based solely on physical connection to a Co-Located 
load. However, the Commission recognized that a generating facility may not be entirely 
committed to a Co-Located Load, but instead in some cases only a “portion of the generating 
facility [will] be designated to serve any Co-Located Load.”60 To conform the definition to the 
Commission’s intent, Constellation recommends that the Commission direct PJM to revise the 
definition to “mean the portion of an existing or planned Generating Facility that the 
Interconnection Customer designates to serve and is physically connected to a Co-Located Load.”

III. 
The Commission Should Require Other Modifications to Ensure Interim NITS 
Provisions Comply with the December 18th Order 
Three other simple modifications to PJM’s proposed Tariff revisions are needed to 
effectuate the December 18th Order’s mandate for Interim Network Integrated Transmission 
Service. First, in Part III of the Tariff, a load’s “option to seek” Interim NITS should be replaced 
with an “option to take.” This modification conforms the Tariff with the December 18th Order, 
which stated that Interim Network Integration Transmission Service “must allow an Eligible 
Customer that has requested NITS on behalf of a Co-Located Load to take non-firm transmission 
service that can be interrupted until the Network Upgrades necessary to provide NITS are 
complete.”61 As revised, Part III of the Tariff would read, “Eligible Customers taking transmission 
service on behalf of Co-Located Load must take one of the following services: (1) Network 
Integration Transmission Service under Tariff, Part III, with the option to take Interim Network 
Integration Transmission Service….” 
Second, Section 28.1 should be revised to clarify that Interim Network Integration 
Transmission Service is available to Eligible Customers taking service on behalf of Co-Located 
Load. We recommend that Section 28.1 read, “Subject to the terms of the Tariff, Part III, Eligible 
Customers taking service on behalf of Co-Located Load may also receive Network Integration 
Transmission Service [with the option to take Interim Network Integration Transmission 
Service.]”62 
 
61 Id. P 200. We also acknowledge that the Commission stated that Interim Network Integration Transmission Service 
“would only be available to the extent PJM determines that it can provide some level of interim service reliably.” 
Id. 
62 Sixty-Day Compliance Filing at 62.

19 
Third, similar to Section 28.1, Section 29.1 should be revised to read, “Any Eligible 
Customer taking service on behalf of Co-Located Load must also satisfy these conditions to 
receive Network Integration Transmission Service [and/or Interim Network Integration 
Transmission Service].”63 
IV. 
The Commission Should Clarify that Capacity Serving Non-Firm Load Need Not Delist 
and Direct Further Compliance  
PJM’s proposed Tariff revisions direct that the “Project Developer shall provide 
Transmission Provider with all information needed to perform the Necessary Studies” including 
“the amount of reduction to Capacity Interconnection Rights to facilitate the Co-Located Load 
configuration.”64 PJM states this revision complies with the December 18th Order’s statement that 
“an existing generating facility may not begin serving Co-Located Load that is not Network Load 
until it has delisted its [Capacity Interconnection Rights] for the portion of the generating facility 
to be designated to serve any Co-Located Load that is not receiving NITS.”65 
As Constellation explained in its Request for Clarification, the Commission should clarify 
that it did not intend to require a capacity resource to delist even when it has no obligation to serve 
the Co-Located Load and remains fully capable of serving the grid during capacity emergencies.66 
Indeed, the Commission should encourage arrangements in which Co-Located Load can receive 
non-NITS service (such as non-firm contract service) and also curtail its reliance on the Co-
Located generator during capacity emergencies. Such an arrangement is consistent with existing

PJM rules; enables the speedy interconnection of new data center load, important to our economic 
competitiveness and national security; allows the co-location of that load, minimizing the need for 
grid upgrades; and allows for the continued availability of the co-located generator to serve the 
grid when it is needed to ensure resource adequacy. Forcing such capacity nevertheless to delist 
would needlessly remove available capacity from serving the grid, inconsistent with PJM 
precedent.67 
Upon granting Constellation’s requested clarification or rehearing, the Commission could 
direct PJM to revise its Tariff to clarify that only when capacity will serve physically firm 
commitments must Project Developers declare the amount of reduction to Capacity

21 
CONCLUSION 
For the reasons stated above, Constellation respectfully requests that the Commission grant 
this protest and accept these comments and direct further compliance to ensure PJM’s Tariff 
follows the directives of the December 18th Order.
